hero.h1: How do we deliver the best training possible today?
hero.intro: A working handbook for people who design and run training. Each practice says what to do first, then why it works and where that comes from.

toolkitTile.heading: Find methods, recipes and ideas for sessions

mistakes.heading: Common mistakes, and what to do instead
mistakes.status: Draft wording. Each "why" needs its citation checked when the linked topic is written.

items.title: Ordering a course for a problem training cannot fix.
items.why: If people could do the job when it really mattered, the cause is tools, incentives or unclear expectations. No course changes those.
items.instead: Ask whether they could do it if they had to. If yes, fix the environment. If no, train.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Skill problem or will problem?

items.title: Running a one-off event with nothing before or after it.
items.why: Whether learning shows up at work depends on the manager and the workplace as much as on the session.
items.instead: Plan the manager conversation, the first use at work and the follow-up before you plan the day.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: The transfer problem

items.title: Counting attendance and satisfaction as proof it worked.
items.why: How much people enjoyed a session says little about what they learned or what they now do.
items.instead: Decide up front what people should do differently, and go and look for that.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 6: Evaluation models, used critically

items.title: Teaching the AI tool without changing the work around it.
items.why: People go back to the same workflow, access and targets, so the old way of working wins.
items.instead: Pick one real workflow, redesign it with the tool, and train people on that.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 7: Training people for an AI world

items.title: Filling slides with text, then reading them out.
items.why: Reading and listening to the same words at once overloads a very limited working memory.
items.instead: One claim per slide, with evidence. Say the detail; do not show it.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: The multimedia design principles

items.title: Designing around learning styles.
items.why: There is no good evidence that matching teaching to a preferred style improves learning.
items.instead: Match the medium to the content: show a process, describe a principle, practise a skill.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Drop learning styles and the other big myths

items.title: Leaving managers out of it.
items.why: What a manager expects and reinforces afterwards is one of the strongest influences on whether new skills get used.
items.instead: Give managers three things to do: one before, one during, one after.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Stakeholders, managers and the transfer environment

items.title: Cramming everything into one long day.
items.why: Practice packed into one sitting feels productive and fades fast. The gaps between sessions are where memory settles.
items.instead: Cut the content, split the day, and come back to the key ideas later.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Make practice harder in the ways that help

items.title: Choosing the medium before the goal.
items.why: A video, an app or a headset does not teach by itself. The method does, whatever carries it.
items.instead: Start from what people must be able to do, then pick the medium that makes that practice possible.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: Choosing the medium

items.title: Writing objectives that say "understand" or "be aware of".
items.why: Nobody can observe understanding, so nobody can design for it or check it.
items.instead: Write what people will be able to do, under what conditions, and how well.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Learning objectives and alignment

items.title: Moving a classroom session onto a video call unchanged.
items.why: Video calls tire people for specific reasons: constant close-up eye contact, seeing yourself, sitting still, and working harder to read faces.
items.instead: Keep live time for interaction only. Move content to pre-work and design against the fatigue.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 4: Why remote learning tires people

items.title: Running tick-box compliance training.
items.why: It is designed to prove that something happened, not to change what people do.
items.instead: Name the behaviour that matters and measure that.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 6: Measuring behaviour and results

items.title: Adding fun extras that teach nothing.
items.why: Interesting but irrelevant material pulls attention away from the point and lowers learning.
items.instead: Cut anything that does not serve the objective, however engaging it is.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: The multimedia design principles

items.title: Judging a session by how smoothly it went.
items.why: How fluent people look in the room is a poor guide to what they will remember next week.
items.instead: Check again after a delay, when the easy familiarity has worn off.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Do not trust how fluent the room looks

items.title: Assuming people will pick it up on the job.
items.why: Experience without feedback levels off. Years in a role are not the same as getting better at it.
items.instead: Build in practice at the edge of ability, with someone giving feedback.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Build practice at the edge of ability

items.title: Publishing AI-written training that nobody qualified has checked.
items.why: AI tools produce confident errors and repeat bias from their training data.
items.instead: Use AI for the first draft and keep a named person responsible for every output.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 7: Risks, guardrails and governance

items.title: Packing a retreat from breakfast to midnight.
items.why: Memory is consolidated during sleep. Long days cut into the thing the retreat depends on.
items.instead: Protect sleep and leave gaps in the schedule on purpose.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

findings.heading: Findings worth designing around
findings.guideLink: How we rate evidence, A to E
findings.status: Tiers are provisional. Citations are author and year from memory of the literature; verify each before publishing.

items.title: Recalling something beats reading it again.
items.use: Open each session with a short recall task before any new content.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Designing practice

items.title: Practice spread over days beats one long session.
items.use: Split a full day into shorter sessions with gaps, or add follow-ups a few days and weeks later.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Spaced reinforcement after the event

items.title: Working memory holds about four things at once.
items.use: Introduce new ideas a few at a time and group them before adding more.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Design for a very small working memory

items.title: Matching teaching to a learning style does not improve learning.
items.use: Stop sorting people by style. Choose the medium that suits the content.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: The myths

items.title: Satisfaction scores say little about what was learned.
items.use: Keep the feedback form short and measure behaviour separately.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 6: Evaluation models, used critically

items.title: Waiting a few seconds after a question gets better answers.
items.use: Ask, then count to three in your head before you speak again.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 4: Facilitating versus presenting

items.title: Beginners learn more from worked examples than from solving problems cold.
items.use: Show a full solved example first, then remove the support step by step.
items.source: Sweller, 1988; Sweller, van Merriënboer and Paas, 1998.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Cut the load that teaches nothing

items.title: Help that suits beginners can hold experienced people back.
items.use: In a mixed room, give the experienced people the harder version, not the same support.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Cut the load that teaches nothing

items.title: How well people perform in the session is a poor guide to what they will keep.
items.use: Do not judge a method by how the room looks. Test again later.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Do not trust how fluent the room looks

items.title: People feel they learn more from easy study than from hard practice. It is the other way round.
items.use: Tell learners why the harder practice is there, or they will resist it.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Make practice harder in the ways that help

items.title: Mixing related problem types beats practising one type at a time.
items.use: Once the basics are in, shuffle the practice so people have to work out which approach fits.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Designing practice

items.title: A specific if-then plan makes follow-through more likely.
items.use: End a session with each person writing: when this happens, I will do that.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 5: Designing for transfer

items.title: Sleep after learning strengthens memory.
items.use: On multi-day programmes, protect the nights and revisit yesterday first thing.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Protect sleep on multi-day programmes

items.title: Hours of practice explain only part of expertise.
items.use: Never promise mastery from time served. Design the quality of the practice.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Build practice at the edge of ability

items.title: Feedback on the task helps. Praise for the person does little.
items.use: Tell people where they are, how it is going and what to do next.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 2: Accessibility, fairness and feedback

items.title: Interesting but irrelevant extras reduce learning.
items.use: Cut the anecdote, the clip or the graphic that does not serve the point.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 3: The multimedia design principles

items.title: Teams that feel safe report more mistakes, not fewer.
items.use: Show your own mistakes early, and treat a wrong answer as useful.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 1: Make it safe to be wrong out loud

items.title: Well-designed tutoring software produces moderate, real gains.
items.use: Expect a useful improvement from adaptive tools, not a transformation, and only when the design is good.
items.boardLinkLabel: Stage 7: Adaptive tutoring and the honest evidence

myths.heading: Things the industry repeats that do not hold up
myths.intro: Popular claims, each traced back to where it came from, with a verdict. Flick through a few.

items.claim: "Only 10% of training transfers to the job."
items.why: The figure traces to a 1982 magazine article that offered it as a guess. Transfer is a real problem, but nobody measured 10%.

items.claim: "Teach people in their own learning style."
items.why: People have preferences, but studies do not show that matching teaching to them improves learning.
The original studies were about conveying feelings with single words. They say nothing about communication in general.

items.claim: "It takes 10,000 hours to become an expert."
items.why: Practice matters a great deal, but the amount of it explains only part of the difference between people.

items.claim: "We remember 10% of what we read and 90% of what we teach."
items.verdict: Verdict: no research behind the numbers.
items.why: The percentages in the "learning pyramid" trace to no study. They were added later to a diagram that had no numbers. Draft: source not checked yet.

items.claim: "Spend 70% on experience, 20% on social, 10% on courses."
items.verdict: Verdict: a reminder, not a formula.
items.why: The numbers come from self-report surveys in the 1980s. Most learning does happen outside courses. Nobody measured 70, 20 and 10. Draft: source not checked yet.

items.claim: "Attention spans are down to eight seconds."
items.why: Attention depends on interest, difficulty and design. There is no fixed span to shrink. Draft: source not checked yet.
Differences come from experience, role and setting, not from the year someone was born. Draft: source not checked yet.

items.claim: "AI tutoring delivers a two sigma gain."
items.why: The figure is one 1984 result for one-to-one human tutoring and has been hard to repeat. Well-designed tutoring systems show moderate gains. Draft: source not checked yet.
We use virtually all of the brain. Draft: source not checked yet.
The two halves of the brain do specialise. People are not one type or the other. Draft: source not checked yet.
The original finding was narrow and short-lived. It does not raise intelligence in any lasting way. Draft: source not checked yet.
The well-known study was repeated and the effect was not found. Putting ideas in your own words is the part that helps. Draft: source not checked yet.
Growing up with technology does not change how people learn, or make them skilled with it. Draft: source not checked yet.

items.claim: "High satisfaction scores show the training worked."
items.why: How much people liked a course relates only weakly to what they learned. Draft: source not checked yet.

myths.unwrittenWhy: This claim is on the list to trace and check. Nothing is said about it until that is done.

cases.heading: Who does this well

items.name: Toyota
items.what: Teach any job in four steps: prepare the worker, show the job, let them try it, follow up.
items.why: Demonstration, immediate practice, correction on the spot.
items.borrow: Break the task into steps and key points before you teach it.

items.name: Commercial aviation
items.what: Crews rehearse rare emergencies together in simulators, and come back to do it again on a schedule.
items.why: Realistic practice, feedback, and refreshers spaced over a career.
items.borrow: Rehearse the rare, costly moments, and schedule the refresher.

items.name: Harvard Business School
items.what: Students prepare a real business problem, then argue in class for what they would do.
items.why: People commit to an answer, defend it, and hear it challenged.
items.borrow: Make people commit to a decision before you discuss it.

candidatesToResearch: McDonald's Hamburger University (corporate academy at scale)
cases.selectionRule: Publicly documented, a clear mechanism, some evidence of results beyond their own marketing.
